misconceptions.description: Structuring the capstone talk as a screen-by-screen tour of features instead of an argument that moves from problem to decision to evidence
misconceptions.trigger: narrative lists 'here is the home screen, here is the quiz' with no problem driving the order
misconceptions.feedback: Organize the narrative as an argument: the problem, the decisions you made, and the evidence they worked. A feature tour is not a defense.

misconceptions.description: Putting the full spoken script on the slides and reading it aloud, which violates the redundancy principle and overloads the audience
misconceptions.trigger: slides are dense paragraphs the presenter reads verbatim
misconceptions.feedback: Slides carry the visual evidence; the spoken narrative carries the argument. Identical text in both channels increases load and disengages the committee.

misconceptions.description: Asserting that the design works without including an evidence beat (tryout result, alignment trace, theory link) for each major claim
misconceptions.trigger: narrative says 'learners found it engaging' with no source for the claim
misconceptions.feedback: Pair each effectiveness claim with an evidence beat: a tryout observation, an alignment trace, or a theory link the committee can probe.

misconceptions.description: Having AI generate the entire presentation narrative and reading it without checking that the claims match the actual project and that the presenter can defend them
misconceptions.trigger: presenter cannot answer a follow-up because the AI script contained claims the project does not support
misconceptions.feedback: AI can outline a narrative arc, but verify every claim against your own project and rehearse so you can defend it, not just recite it.
